item.title: Bayesian Structured-Sparsity Method Recovers Compact CNN Architectures
item.description:
Bayesian Structured-Sparsity Method Recovers Compact CNN Architectures

Researchers have introduced SoU-RHS, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure designed to recover compact convolutional neural network architectures from overparameterized reference models. The method addresses the memory, computation, and deployment costs associated with highly parameterized networks while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

🔍 Overview

  • SoU-RHS augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with a Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (SoU-SGL)
  • The procedure sharpens separation between active and inactive filters, enabling architecture recovery
  • Evaluated across standard image-classification benchmarks

🧩 How it works

  • Combines Bayesian shrinkage (RHS) with a novel global-local sparsity mechanism (SoU-SGL)
  • Operates as a structured-sparsity procedure targeting filter-level pruning
  • Identifies compact structures adapted to the data rather than compressing each initial model separately

⚙️ Key details

  • Stability property: Across different overparameterized starting widths and a reasonable range of pruning thresholds, SoU-RHS recovers compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation
  • Performance: Recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines while maintaining competitive accuracy
  • Metrics: Achieves lower negative log-likelihood in every evaluated configuration and generally lower expected calibration error

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a principled Bayesian approach to architecture recovery from overparameterized CNNs
  • Stability across initial widths suggests the method identifies intrinsic data-adapted structure
  • Improves uncertainty quantification (lower NLL and ECE) alongside compression

#Bayesian #StructuredSparsity #CNN #ArchitectureRecovery #ImageClassification #MachineLearning

Source: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs

item.title: GauntletScore achieves top accuracy on LLM-AggreFact benchmark
item.description:
GauntletScore achieves top accuracy on LLM-AggreFact benchmark

🧩 How it works

GauntletScore is an evidence engine that puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers. It records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. The system combines these measurements using a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. Unlike single-model checkers, the engine records the evidence behind every verdict.

🚀 Key details

The few rules and thresholds for the engine were set on the benchmark’s development split. The full test split was run once on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. The results show the following:

  • Achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy on the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), matching the leaderboard’s top score.
  • Beats two of its three readers (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points when tested alone.
  • Without the AggreFact-CNN component, the leads over single readers are 0.90 and 1.32 points.
  • The 95% interval for the engine’s score is 78.47 to 80.53.

The engine performs best on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format resembling regulated writing. It scores 76.45 on this specific task, compared to 70.1 for the next best system.

💡 Why it matters

Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text. Currently, the strongest published checkers are single models. GauntletScore offers an alternative that records the specific evidence behind every verdict, a capability single models do not provide.

#LLMAggreFact #FactChecking #AI #Bayesian

Source: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
